title: Remember
hook: memory is a commandment in Judaism
carry: a memory that leads to doing

segments.voice: Yesterday, the yahrzeit, a candle on the Hebrew date, and the line remember the date. Did you write one date down where you'll find it? Today, the word underneath that candle. Day one thousand fifty-six.

Can you order someone to remember? You can tell a person to stand up, or to sit down, or to be quiet. But memory seems to come and go on its own. A song on the radio brings back a summer. A smell brings back a grandmother's hallway. Nobody commands that. And yet the Torah does exactly this. Again and again, it doesn't say try to remember, or it would be nice to remember. It says, in the form of a command: remember. Today's word is that command, and it's one Hebrew word: zachor.
screen: `CAN YOU ORDER A MEMORY?` → `A SONG, A SMELL, A HALLWAY.` → `THE TORAH SAYS: REMEMBER.`

segments.voice: Zachor is the command form of the Hebrew verb for remembering. It sits right inside the Ten Commandments in Exodus: "Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy." Notice what follows the remembering. To keep it. Memory in the Torah isn't a mood. It leads somewhere. The pattern starts with God. In the flood story, the text says: "And God remembered Noah." And the next thing that happens is a wind over the earth, and the waters begin to go down. In the Torah, when God remembers, something moves. That's the shape of zachor. Remembering is the first half of an act. Moses, near the end of his life, sings to the people: "Remember the days of old." Ask your father, he says, and he will tell you; your elders, and they will explain. Memory isn't stored in a book alone. It's passed hand to hand. There's a harder zachor too. Deuteronomy says: "Remember what Amalek did unto thee by the way as ye came forth out of Egypt." Amalek attacked the weak and weary at the back of the line, and the passage closes with "thou shalt not forget." On the Sabbath before Purim, tradition reads those verses aloud in synagogue, and that Sabbath is called Shabbat Zachor. Remembering, there, includes remembering cruelty, so as not to look away from it. That word carries all the way to now. In the Yizkor memorial prayers, in Holocaust remembrance, in the candle from yesterday, the command keeps working. Shabbat, the road out of Egypt, the people who came before, what was done to the weak: in each, the Torah pairs remembering with doing. Today's line is one word: remember.
screen: `REMEMBER THE SABBATH, TO KEEP IT.` · `GOD REMEMBERED NOAH, AND A WIND.` · `REMEMBER THE DAYS OF OLD.` · `REMEMBER WHAT AMALEK DID.` · then, large: `REMEMBER.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: write down one memory. The writing comes right after the bell. For now, sit and breathe, and let one memory rise. Something you were told by an older person, or something you saw that you don't want lost. Hold it in detail: where you were, what the light was like, the words someone used. Ask Moses's question of it: who told me this, and who will I tell? If you pray, you can give thanks in your own words for the people who handed it to you. When the bell sounds, write it down, even in three plain lines. The bell holds the time.
Zachor. Remember: the Torah's command, for Shabbat, for the days of old, for what was done to the weak, a memory that leads to action. Today's word.
Your line: a memory that leads to doing. Today, read the memory you wrote to one person, or send it to them, so it lives in two places. Day one thousand fifty-six.

howItsDone: Jews keep the command to remember through Shabbat, the Passover seder, the reading of the Amalek verses on Shabbat Zachor before Purim, Yizkor memorial prayers, yahrzeit candles and Holocaust remembrance.

notes: Claims rule: no dates or counts. 'Ten Commandments' is the traditional name of Exodus 20 (Aseret ha-Dibrot); please confirm wording.
Deuteronomy 32:7 second half ('ask thy father... thine elders') paraphrased; first phrase quoted. JPS 1917 wording of all quotations should be checked word for word.
Shabbat Zachor described as the Sabbath before Purim on which the Amalek verses are read. Please confirm.
Amalek attacking 'the weak and weary at the back of the line' paraphrases Deuteronomy 25:18. The Amalek theme is handled without applying it to any modern people; please confirm the framing.
'Zachor is the command form of the Hebrew verb for remembering': grammatical description (also infinitive absolute in Exodus 20:8). Please confirm the simplification.
